category: file host with paid premium tier (English UI, crypto checkout)

free_tier.stated: 'Upload files up to 5 GB each without any restrictions' and 'Long-term Storage - We promise to keep your files as long-term in our servers without any premium or subscription'.
free_tier.notes: The 5 GB is a per-file upload cap, not a total. The site claims unlimited storage on the free tier.

per_object_cap.stated: 5 GB per file free; 'Upload Up to 10 GB' on premium
per_object_cap.notes: The premium page states the 10 GB figure; the 5 GB free figure is from the site's own feature list.

retention.stated: 'Very Long-term Files Storage - Your files are safely stored for a long time'. No day count, no inactivity rule published.

egress.terms: Premium adds 'One-Click Direct Download', 'No Blog Redirection', 'No Banners & Pop-Up Ads' and 'Maximum Download Speed ... high-priority access to bandwidth'. No byte allowance and no per-GB price is published.

interface_detail: Upload page plus direct links. No API documentation was found on the pages read; the site markets 'direct links to share files instantly' rather than an API.
tooling: The z_o_o_m File & Image Uploader lists uploadflix.com with account support, which is the practical upload path for batch work. Downloads are plain HTTP and take a download manager.
chaining: A free host with unlimited storage and no expiry is the cheapest place to park an archive; the 5 GB per-file cap decides chunking, and premium is only needed to remove the blog interstitial that breaks scripted downloads.

limits.value: 5 GB per file on free, 10 GB on premium

limits_note: No download volume is published at any tier. The premium page sells speed and ad removal, not gigabytes, which suggests the limit is on the download path rather than on stored bytes.
binding_note: For a 10 TiB archive the 5 GB free cap forces 2,000 objects; that is a chunking cost, not a blocker. No byte allowance is published, so nothing documents a volume failure at 1 TiB/month.
price_per_tb_month: USD 10 per month claimed, USD 48 per year claimed (reported from the vendor page as indexed, not read live)

identity_cost.detail: Account creation with email. Premium checkout was described by the vendor page only through its payment-method line: 'Bitcoin, USDT (TRC/ERC-20), Ethereum, LiteCoin'. No card processor appears in that list, so a buyer holding only a card may not be able to pay.

reliability_note: The brand runs across at least four hostnames (uploadflix.com, 1uploadflix.net, uploadflix.cc, dl.uploadflix.com) and one of them returned a Cloudflare 522 in a search result, which is the failure mode a parked archive cares about. Premium is sold for crypto only, so a refund is not a practical path.
confidence_note: The feature list, the 5 GB free cap and the 10 GB premium cap were read from the vendor's own pages today. The price and the payment-method list come from the search engine's index of the same vendor page: the live page renders those blocks client-side and returned no numbers. Opening the checkout would move the price to documented.

evidence.proved: 'Upload files up to 5 GB each without any restrictions', 'Long-term Storage ... without any premium or subscription', 'Generate direct links ... no registration required'
the nine premium benefits, including 'Upload Up to 10 GB', 'Unlimited Cloud Storage' and 'Very Long-term Files Storage'

'Premium Cost: $10/Month Only. 1-Year Premium: $48 (60% Off Limited Time Offer)' and 'Payment Methods: Bitcoin, USDT (TRC/ERC-20), Ethereum, LiteCoin' - indexed text of the vendor page, not the rendered page
the uploader's changelog entry 'uploadflix.com, uqload.cx' with account support, evidence the host is used by bulk uploaders

notes: UploadFlix is not a Portuguese- or Spanish-language service; it surfaced under Portuguese queries because Brazilian link generators list it. It is recorded here because question - what does the local scene actually use - cannot be answered without the hosts the generators carry.

extras.price_status: reported from index; live page renders client-side
